property_summary: For any interfaceId, the reference contract returns true for IERC165's interfaceId (0x01ffc9a7) iff asked, i.e., supportsInterface(type(IERC165).interfaceId) always returns true for the reference C, whereas the mutant returns false for that interfaceId.

For every bytes4 x, C.supportsInterface(x) returns true when x == type(IERC165).interfaceId if and only if the contract implements ERC165; the reference returns true for IERC165's id for all inputs, while the mutant returns false for that id, so there exists an x (specifically IERC165's id) where the return differs.

For every bytes4 interfaceId, the reference contract C returns true when asked about IERC165's interfaceId (type(IERC165).interfaceId) via supportsInterface (i.e., it reports ERC165 support), whereas the mutant returns false for that specific interfaceId; the test fuzzes an interfaceId and asserts that calling supportsInterface with that id never reverts and that for the particular IERC165 id the call returns true (so the mutant fails for that id).

For every bytes4 interfaceId, calling supportsInterface(interfaceId) on the reference C never reverts and in particular returns true when asked about IERC165's interfaceId; the mutant that drops IERC165 support will return false for type(IERC165).interfaceId, violating this rule for that input.

For every bytes4 interfaceId the reference C reports support for IERC165.interfaceId via supportsInterface (callable without revert), whereas the mutant that removed ERC165 support will return false for type(IERC165).interfaceId, so there exists an interfaceId (the IERC165 id) where the return differs.

For every 4-byte interface id, the reference contract returns supportsInterface(true) exactly when the id equals IERC165's interface id or when a parent supports it (here only IERC165), while the mutant inverts that equality causing some ids (not IERC165) to incorrectly return true; the test fuzzes an interfaceId and asserts that supportsInterface(id) returns true iff id == type(IERC165).interfaceId (reference behavior) — the mutant will fail for some ids.

For every 4-byte interfaceId input, the reference C.supportsInterface(interfaceId) returns true precisely when interfaceId == type(IERC165).interfaceId (and false otherwise); the mutant inverts that equality and thus returns true for many interfaceIds that are not IERC165, violating this rule for some fuzzed inputs.

For every 4-byte interfaceId input, C.supportsInterface(interfaceId) returns true iff interfaceId == type(IERC165).interfaceId (the reference only recognizes IERC165), but the mutant inverts that equality and thus will return true for many interfaceIds that are not IERC165, breaking the rule for some fuzzed inputs.

For every 4-byte interfaceId, the correct contract returns true from supportsInterface(interfaceId) if and only if interfaceId equals type(IERC165).interfaceId; the mutant inverts that check and will therefore return true for some interfaceIds that are NOT IERC165, violating this iff rule for some fuzzed inputs.

For every 4-byte interfaceId input, the reference contract returns true from supportsInterface(interfaceId) exactly when interfaceId == type(IERC165).interfaceId; the mutant inverts the equality and thus will return true for some interfaceIds that are NOT IERC165, violating this rule for some fuzzed inputs.

For every 4-byte interfaceId, C.supportsInterface(interfaceId) returns true whenever interfaceId equals IERC165 or IAccessControl interface id (as computed by the reference), while the mutant that always returns false will fail this for those interfaceIds; the test fuzzes an interfaceId and asserts that calling supportsInterface does not revert and that when the id equals either IERC165 or IAccessControl id the call returns true (which the mutant breaks).

For every 4-byte interfaceId, the reference C never reverts and, if the id equals either IERC165 or IAccessControl interface id, C.supportsInterface(interfaceId) returns true; the mutant that always returns false violates this by returning false for those ids.

For every 4-byte interfaceId, calling supportsInterface(interfaceId) on the correct contract never reverts and returns true when interfaceId equals type(IERC165).interfaceId or type(IAccessControl).interfaceId; the mutant that always returns false will still not revert but will return false for those interface ids, violating the rule.

For every 4-byte interfaceId, C.supportsInterface(interfaceId) never reverts, and in particular it returns true for the IERC165 interface id (type(IERC165).interfaceId) — the mutant that always returns false breaks this by returning false for that id (so there exists an input where return differs).

For every 4-byte interfaceId the reference C.supportsInterface(interfaceId) call always succeeds (does not revert) and specifically returns true when the interfaceId equals the IAccessControl interface id; the mutant that always returns false will return false for that id, violating the rule for some input.

For every 4-byte interfaceId the correct contract C returns true exactly for the IERC165 and IAccessControl interface ids (i.e. supportsInterface(interfaceId) is true iff interfaceId==type(IERC165).interfaceId or interfaceId==type(IAccessControl).interfaceId), whereas the mutant incorrectly returns true for all interface ids; the test asserts that for any fuzzed bytes4 id, C.supportsInterface(id) returns either true only for the known supported ids or false for others (we check that if supportsInterface(id) is true then id must equal one of the supported interface ids), which the mutant violates for some id.

For any bytes4 interfaceId, if C.supportsInterface(interfaceId) returns true then the id must be either IERC165 or IAccessControl's interface id; the mutant returns true for other ids and thus violates this invariant for some fuzzed id.

For every bytes4 interfaceId, if C.supportsInterface(interfaceId) returns true then that id must be either IERC165 or IAccessControl's interface id; the mutant returns true for other ids and thus violates this invariant for some fuzzed id.

For every bytes4 interfaceId, if C.supportsInterface(interfaceId) returns true then that id must be exactly IERC165 or IAccessControl's interface id; the mutant returns true for other ids, violating this rule for some fuzzed id.

For any bytes4 interfaceId, if c.supportsInterface(interfaceId) returns true then that id must be either type(IERC165).interfaceId or type(IAccessControl).interfaceId; the mutant that always returns true will violate this for some other bytes4 id.

For every (role, account) pair, the reference contract's hasRole returns the stored membership boolean, whereas the mutant inverts that boolean so for some (role, account) the returned value differs (i.e., hasRole(role,account) == !_roles[role].members[account] is false in reference but true in mutant).

For every role/account the reference contract returns hasRole(role, account) == c.getTimestamp(keccak256(abi.encodePacked(role, account)))==0 is NOT used; instead: the general rule is that for any role and account, hasRole(role, account) equals the stored membership boolean (i.e., it returns true exactly when the internal members mapping for that role contains the account); the mutant negates that result, so there exist role/account pairs where hasRole differs between reference and mutant.

For any role and account, hasRole(role, account) returns the stored membership boolean for that role/account (true iff the account is in the role's members); the mutant inverts that return value, so for some fuzzed role/account the returned boolean differs.

For any role and account, hasRole(role, account) returns true exactly when the contract's stored membership mapping contains that account; the mutant inverts that boolean so there exist role/account inputs where hasRole returns the opposite value.

For any (role, account) input, C.hasRole(role, account) returns the actual stored membership boolean for that role/account (true iff the account is in the role's members); the mutant negates that return value so for some fuzzed role/account the returned boolean differs, causing the property to fail.

For every role and account, the real contract returns whether the account has that role per its internal storage (i.e., hasRole(role, account) == C.hasRole reads the stored mapping), whereas the mutant always returns true; thus the invariant is that if an account was never granted a role (and not the contract deployer or configured roles), hasRole must be false — the mutant can return true for some such fuzzed (role,account) pair.
